title: Good Strategy Bad Strategy
author: Richard P. Rumelt
theme: A real strategy is a coherent response to a clearly diagnosed challenge, not a list of goals, slogans or ambitions.
summary: Richard Rumelt argues that the word strategy has been worn down until it means almost anything: a vision statement, a budget target, a set of values or an inspiring speech. Most of what organisations call strategy, he says, is nothing of the kind. A true strategy is a focused answer to a specific challenge, and it is surprisingly rare.

He first describes the marks of bad strategy. One is fluff: grand, abstract language that sounds deep but says little. Another is failing to face the challenge, so the plan never names the actual obstacle. A third is mistaking goals for strategy, as when leaders announce growth targets and call that a plan. A fourth is setting objectives that are either a long, unprioritised wish list or so ambitious that nobody knows how to reach them. Bad strategy often comes from avoiding hard choices, or from the belief that positive thinking alone produces results.

Good strategy, in contrast, has a simple core that Rumelt calls the kernel. It has three parts. A diagnosis explains what is really going on and which difficulty matters most. A guiding policy sets the overall approach for dealing with that difficulty. Coherent actions are coordinated steps that carry out the policy and reinforce one another.

Rumelt then explores sources of strength that good strategies draw on. Leverage comes from concentrating effort where it will have the greatest effect. Proximate objectives are near-term targets that are clear enough to be achieved. Focus, design and the careful fitting together of activities create advantages that rivals find hard to copy. Leaders also gain by noticing shifts in technology or markets early, and by watching for inertia and decay inside their own organisations.

Finally, he treats strategy as a hypothesis to be tested. Leaders should think like scientists, question their own judgments and stay open to evidence. The lasting lesson is that strategy means choosing, and choosing means saying no.
takeaway: Name the critical challenge honestly, choose one guiding approach to it, and back it with coordinated actions.

questions.q: According to Rumelt, what is the main problem with most documents labelled 'strategy'?
options: They are too short to be useful
They are mostly goals, slogans or wish lists rather than a real response to a challenge
They rely too heavily on financial data
They are written by outside consultants
questions.why: Rumelt's central complaint is that much so-called strategy is fluff, goals or ambitions with no actual plan for overcoming an obstacle.

questions.q: What three elements make up the 'kernel' of a good strategy?
options: Vision, mission and values
Budget, timeline and owners
Diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent actions
Goals, metrics and incentives
questions.why: The kernel consists of a diagnosis of the situation, a guiding policy for dealing with it, and coherent actions that carry it out.

questions.q: In Rumelt's terms, what does 'fluff' refer to?
options: Grand, abstract language that sounds profound but says little
Extra resources held in reserve
Minor tactical details in a plan
Optimistic sales forecasts
questions.why: Fluff is superficial, buzzword-heavy language that disguises the absence of real strategic thinking.

questions.q: Why does Rumelt say that announcing an ambitious growth target is not a strategy?
options: Because growth is never a worthy aim
Because targets should only be set by boards
Because targets are always too low
Because a goal states what is wanted, not how the key obstacle will be overcome
questions.why: Mistaking goals for strategy leaves out the diagnosis and the actions needed to get past the real difficulty.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the diagnosis in a good strategy?
options: To assign blame for past failures
To explain what is really going on and identify the critical difficulty
To list every possible risk the organisation faces
To benchmark the company against its competitors' budgets
questions.why: The diagnosis simplifies a complex situation by naming the challenge that matters most.

questions.q: What makes a set of actions 'coherent' in Rumelt's framework?
options: They are coordinated and reinforce one another in support of the guiding policy
They are spread evenly across all departments
They are each approved by a separate committee
They can be completed within one financial year
questions.why: Coherent actions fit together and amplify each other rather than pulling in different directions.

questions.q: What does Rumelt mean by a 'proximate objective'?
options: A long-range vision for the next twenty years
An objective borrowed from a nearby competitor
A near-term target clear and feasible enough to be achieved
A goal set by the nearest level of management
questions.why: Proximate objectives turn a hard situation into a solvable problem that people can act on.

questions.q: Which idea best describes 'leverage' as a source of strategic strength?
options: Borrowing money to fund expansion
Spreading effort thinly across many initiatives
Using personal authority to force agreement
Concentrating effort where it will have the greatest effect
questions.why: Leverage comes from focusing resources on a pivotal point so that a limited effort produces a large result.

questions.q: According to the book, what often causes leaders to produce bad strategy?
options: Avoiding hard choices and hoping that positive thinking will be enough
Spending too much time analysing competitors
Focusing on too few priorities
Relying on scientific methods
questions.why: Rumelt argues that bad strategy often comes from an unwillingness to choose and from a belief that enthusiasm alone brings results.

questions.q: How does Rumelt suggest leaders should treat a strategy once it is formed?
options: As a fixed commitment that must never change
As a confidential document for senior staff only
As a hypothesis to be tested and revised in light of evidence
As a marketing message for customers
questions.why: He encourages leaders to think like scientists, questioning their judgments and learning from results.
